newsitem.title: USA: NYS comptroller says state must create jobs.
newsitem.headline: NYS comptroller says state must create jobs.

text.p: The New York State Comptroller on Thursday faulted the Pataki Administration for not creating more jobs, noting the state for the second year in a row ranked 49th in the nation in job growth.
And the state Comptroller, H. Carl McCall, again faulted the governor and legislature for using "short-sighted," risky one-shot manuevers to close budget gaps.

McCall, who was reviewing the state's finances, said that taxpayers were being hurt by New York's failure to improve its credit rating, which he said was the lowest in the nation, as this has increased the costs of borrowing money.
Noting that the 1996-97 budget relies upon about $1 billion of one-shot items, he projected that next year's budget gap will reach $3 billion.
"More one-shot and backdoor borrowing won't help the state turn its credit rating around," the comptroller said, in prepared remarks.

The tax cuts in the 1996-97 budget will cut revenues by $2 billion in the current fiscal year, McCall said, noting he has yet to see Gov. George Pataki or the legislature develop a long-term plan showing how these reductions will be paid for. Further, he faulted the governor and legislature for not planning how they will close future budget gaps.
McCall concluded that the state's most urgent task is creating jobs, but said it also lacked a long-term plan to accomplish this as well.

The Pataki Administration, pointing to a drop in the unemployment rate, which in August fell to 6 percent, down from 6.9 percent in January 1995, has heralded its success in bringing new jobs to the state.
The governor considers workers' compensation reforms, which are expected to cut the program's costs by 25 percent, as one of the capstones of the legislative session.

The number of people employed in New York State rose above eight million in January 1996, the first time since November 1991, when measured on a seasonally adjusted basis, the state Labor Department said.
The comptroller highlighted several other findings, which follow.
--Only 17 percent of the $30 billion of outstanding debt that was supported by the state in 1996 was approved by voters. They had approved 100 percent of such debt in 1960.
--New York's debt service payments are projected to hit $3.8 billion a year by 2001.
--The state's accumulated deficit in the General Fund was $2.9 billion as of March 1996, while there was an operating surplus of $380 million.
--Between 1990 and 1994, local government debt rose 33 percent.
